lead: Chemical potential μ is the partial molar Gibbs energy of a species. It measures how strongly that species tends to leave a phase. At equilibrium, every species has the same μ in every phase present. If μ differs, matter moves from the phase with higher μ to the phase with lower μ, lowering the total Gibbs energy G at fixed temperature T and pressure P. This one rule explains evaporation, absorption, distillation, and many separations in chemical engineering. It is the foundation for fugacity, activity, and phase-equilibrium calculations.
prereq: You need the fundamental property relation dG = −S dT + V dP (from thermodynamic property relations) and the difference between intensive and extensive variables (from basic concepts and the first law).

blocks.text: For a mixture, Gibbs energy G depends on temperature T, pressure P, and the number of moles n<sub>i</sub> of every species i. Chemical potential μ<sub>i</sub> is the rate at which G changes, per mole of i, when a very small amount of i is added with T, P and all other n<sub>j</sub> held constant.
μ<sub>i</sub> = (∂G/∂n<sub>i</sub>) at fixed T, P, and n<sub>j</sub>
blocks.where: μ<sub>i</sub> is the chemical potential of species i in J/mol or kJ/mol; G is total Gibbs energy in J or kJ; n<sub>i</sub> is moles of i; n<sub>j</sub> means moles of every species except i.

blocks.text: For a pure substance, μi = G/ni, the molar Gibbs energy. In a mixture, μi also depends on composition. Some syllabi simply call μi the partial molar Gibbs energy. Read it as a measure of how strongly species i tends to leave its phase, not of how much i is present. Chapter 5.2 develops partial molar properties in more detail.

sections.h3: The fundamental equation with changing moles

blocks.text: For a closed system of fixed amount and composition, the fundamental property relation is dG = −S dT + V dP. When moles can change, add one term for each species.
dG = −S dT + V dP + Σ μ<sub>i</sub> dn<sub>i</sub>
blocks.where: dG is the small change in total Gibbs energy; S is total entropy; T is absolute temperature; V is total volume; P is pressure; μ<sub>i</sub> is chemical potential of species i; dn<sub>i</sub> is the small change in moles of i; Σ means sum over all species.

blocks.text: You can derive this by writing G as a function of T, P, n1, n2, ... and taking the total differential. The T derivative is −S. The P derivative is V. The ni derivative defines μi. At fixed T and P, dG = Σ μi dni. This is the working equation for mass transfer between phases. The μi are not independent at fixed T and P; the Gibbs-Duhem equation in Chapter 5.3 links their changes.

Take two phases α and β. For each species i, equilibrium requires μ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> = μ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>. This holds for a pure component and for every component in a mixture. Temperature equality stops heat flow. Pressure equality stops volume change. Chemical potential equality stops net mass transfer.

If μ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> > μ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup>, move dn moles of i from β to α. Then dG = (μ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> − μ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>) dn. The right side is negative, so G falls. Spontaneous transfer is from higher μ to lower μ. When the two values are equal, dG = 0 and there is no net transfer. The equality is dynamic: molecules still cross, but both directions balance. At fixed T and P the equilibrium state is the one with the lowest total G, so at equilibrium no small transfer of any species between the phases can lower G further.

examples.question: At 300 K, liquid A has μ<sub>A</sub>(liquid) = 100.0 kJ/mol and vapour A has μ<sub>A</sub>(vapour) = 101.5 kJ/mol. 0.010 mol of A moves from vapour to liquid at constant T and P. Find ΔG for this transfer. State whether the transfer is spontaneous.
steps: Identify the donor and receiver. Vapour is the donor with μ<sub>vap</sub> = 101.5 kJ/mol. (Only the difference between the two values matters; both are measured from the same reference state.) Liquid is the receiver with μ<sub>liq</sub> = 100.0 kJ/mol.
For a transfer of dn = 0.010 mol from vapour to liquid, the liquid gains Δn<sub>liq</sub> = +0.010 mol and the vapour loses Δn<sub>vap</sub> = −0.010 mol.

At fixed T and P, ΔG = μ<sub>liq</sub> Δn<sub>liq</sub> + μ<sub>vap</sub> Δn<sub>vap</sub>. The 0.010 mol is small, so both μ values stay practically constant while it moves; a large transfer would change the compositions and need an integral.
Convert to joules: ΔG = −0.015 kJ × 1000 J/kJ = −15 J.
ΔG is negative, so the vapour-to-liquid transfer is spontaneous at these conditions.
examples.answer: ΔG = −0.015 kJ = −15 J, so 0.010 mol of A moves from vapour to liquid spontaneously.
examples.check:
mu_liq = 100.0  # kJ/mol
mu_vap = 101.5  # kJ/mol
n = 0.010  # mol
dG_kJ = (mu_liq - mu_vap) * n
dG_J = dG_kJ * 1000.0
print(dG_kJ)
print(dG_J)

traps: Using μ only for pure substances. In a mixture, μ depends on composition. A higher μ means higher escaping tendency, not higher concentration.
Setting only T and P equal for phase equilibrium. Thermal and mechanical equilibrium are not enough; every species must also have equal μ in all phases.
Making a sign slip in ΔG. For transfer from a donor to a receiver, use ΔG = (μ<sub>receiver</sub> − μ<sub>donor</sub>) dn. Spontaneous transfer needs a negative result.
Confusing μ with molar Gibbs energy for a mixture. They are equal only for a pure substance; for a mixture, μ is the partial molar Gibbs energy.
Forgetting units. μ in kJ/mol times n in mol gives kJ. Convert to J only at the end if the question asks for joules.

quiz.q: Define the chemical potential μ<sub>i</sub> of species i in a mixture.
quiz.a: μ<sub>i</sub> = (∂G/∂n<sub>i</sub>) at fixed T, P, and all other n<sub>j</sub>. It is the rate of change of the total Gibbs energy per mole of i added, with temperature, pressure and the moles of every other species fixed.

quiz.q: Why does a species move from a phase with higher chemical potential to a phase with lower chemical potential at fixed T and P?
quiz.a: For transfer of dn moles from β to α, dG = (μ<sub>α</sub> − μ<sub>β</sub>) dn. If μ<sub>β</sub> > μ<sub>α</sub>, then dG is negative, so G falls. A spontaneous process at fixed T and P lowers G, so matter moves from higher μ to lower μ.

quiz.q: At 350 K, μ<sub>A</sub>(liquid) = 80.0 kJ/mol and μ<sub>A</sub>(vapour) = 81.2 kJ/mol. 0.020 mol of A moves from vapour to liquid. Find ΔG in kJ and J.
quiz.a: ΔG = (μ<sub>liq</sub> − μ<sub>vap</sub>) n = (80.0 − 81.2)(0.020) = (−1.2)(0.020) = −0.024 kJ. In joules, ΔG = −24 J. The transfer is spontaneous.

quiz.q: A liquid mixture has x<sub>A</sub> = 0.9 and μ<sub>A</sub>(liquid) = 50 kJ/mol. The vapour in contact has y<sub>A</sub> = 0.1 and μ<sub>A</sub>(vapour) = 52 kJ/mol. Decide whether A condenses or evaporates. Explain in one line.
quiz.a: Vapour A has higher μ (52 kJ/mol) than liquid A (50 kJ/mol). A moves from vapour to liquid, so A condenses. Concentration alone does not decide direction; chemical potential does.

quiz.q: Two phases α and β are not yet in equilibrium: μ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> = μ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> + 2.0 kJ/mol. In which direction does species i transfer, and what is ΔG when 0.050 mol moves that way?
quiz.a: μ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> is higher than μ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> by 2.0 kJ/mol. Species i transfers from α to β, the lower chemical potential. ΔG = (μ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> − μ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup>)(0.050 mol) = (−2.0)(0.050) = −0.10 kJ = −100 J.

quiz.q: Write the fundamental relation for dG of an open system with changing moles.
quiz.a: dG = −S dT + V dP + Σ μ<sub>i</sub> dn<sub>i</sub>, where S is total entropy, V is total volume, μ<sub>i</sub> is chemical potential, and dn<sub>i</sub> is the change in moles of species i.

quiz.q: Why are equal temperature and equal pressure not enough for phase equilibrium in a mixture?
quiz.a: Equal T stops heat flow and equal P stops volume change. Matter can still move if a species has different chemical potential in the two phases. Equilibrium also needs μ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> = μ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> for every species i.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators such as Aspen Plus and DWSIM solve phase equilibrium by minimising Gibbs energy with chemical potential models, not by hand. Research uses molecular simulation and COSMO-RS to predict μ in mixtures where activity models fail. Electrochemical potential adds an electrical term to μ; it controls battery voltage, fuel cells, and corrosion.
